source.title: Attention, not scale, drives human-AI alignment in multimodal language prediction
source.authors: Viktor Kewenig; Andrew Kyle Lampinen; Samuel A. Nastase; Christopher J. Edwards; Quitterie D'Elascombe; Akilles Richardt; Jeremy I. Skipper; G. Vigliocco

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure references and mathematical symbols are garbled, but the relevant results are also stated in text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how model size relates to performance on a human–model alignment task, using behavioral alignment rather than held-out pretraining loss or the original scaling-law fitting method.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fit scaling laws or test held-out cross-entropy loss across parameter, token, or compute scales. Its direct size-related results concern alignment with human predictability ratings. Perplexity and predictive-entropy measurements are included as related findings, but they do not test a scaling law.
record.test_reason: Within-family size comparisons of CLIP models (three ResNet and three ViT sizes) report how model size relates to a downstream measure, human–model agreement on word predictability. This bears weakly on V6 in a new setting. The cross-family comparison (FLAVA, LLaMA, GPT-4) is confounded by architecture and training, and GPT-4's size is unknown. No loss-scaling fits are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that visual context raises model–human alignment in all architectures and that attention, especially cross-modal attention, rather than parameter count drives alignment. They base the 'not scale' claim mainly on the confounded cross-family comparison. Their own CLIP regression still lists model size among the predictors.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses human-alignment ratings, multimodal model comparisons, and CLIP size-family analyses rather than fitting held-out loss against parameter, token, or compute counts.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varied with predictability percentile and architecture; the ResNet size trend was concentrated at the 25th percentile and negligible at the 90th, while ViT size effects were small and non-significant.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding visual input slightly and non-significantly lowered perplexity on the study stimuli for FLAVA and LLaMA-Adapter. RoBERTa-base had lower perplexity than both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Visual context modestly changes stimulus perplexity; this is unrelated to loss scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: The best-matching frame reduced predictive entropy for FLAVA (0.26 bits), LLaMA-Adapter (~0.17 bits) and BLIP (0.24 bits).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Visual context constrains multimodal models' predictive distributions.

record.problems: The model-size comparisons are not a controlled scale sweep across one model family and training setup; the cross-model comparison mixes architectures and training regimes. Size-family effects on alignment were small or non-significant. The reported perplexities are on the study stimuli, not a stated held-out pretraining corpus.
record.rows_left_out: Attention-ablation, gaze-alignment, semantic-representation, and other attention results were not extracted because they do not measure model scale or downstream predictability as a function of scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; any fitted or predictable scaling trend; scale ranges beyond three sizes per family; standard downstream benchmarks.
Not tested: architecture comparisons concern alignment, not loss at fixed parameters.
Not tested: multimodal models are used, but no power-law form is fitted.

missing.what: Comprehensive regression (architecture, size rank, percentile, interactions; R²=62.8%, F(7,16)=3.85, p=0.012) naming model size among the principal predictors of human–model agreement. This qualifies the 'no size effect' reading.
missing.locator: Results, Prediction 2, paragraph after within-family analyses

missing.what: Per-model CLIP correlations with bootstrap CIs: RN50×4 r=0.001, RN50×64 r=0.238 (25th) / 0.170 (90th), ViT-32 r=0.396 / 0.229.

record.verdict_notes: The headline 'no impact of parameter size' rests on comparing FLAVA, LLaMA-7B and GPT-4, which differ in family, training and measurement method. I treated that comparison as uninformative for V6. The within-family CLIP evidence covers only three sizes per family on a human-alignment measure, so the verdicts are weak and setting-specific.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or parameter/token/compute sweep of held-out pretraining loss.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
Architecture comparisons concern human–model alignment, not loss at a fixed parameter count.
The study uses multimodal models, but does not test whether power-law loss scaling holds in multimodal or other training regimes.
Tests model size against human–model alignment on this prediction task; does not test downstream task performance as a function of pretraining loss or across a broad range of tasks.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending.

rows.subject: FLAVA-full, LLaMA-7B/LLaMA-Adapter, and GPT-4 (aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: FLAVA-full: 1.3 billion parameters; LLaMA-7B: 7B; GPT-4: more parameters than LLaMA, exact count not stated
rows.stage_stated: pretrained; LLaMA-Adapter visual adapter was fine-tuned
rows.operation_detail: Compared model–human alignment in the multimodal prediction condition across models of different sizes
rows.measure: Model–human alignment as a function of parameter size
rows.value: Parameter size did not seem to significantly impact alignment; FLAVA outperformed the larger LLaMA and GPT-4 models, while GPT-4 and FLAVA showed no significant difference in alignment
rows.note: Aggregate comparison as reported by the authors; model families and multimodal training setups differ, so this is not a controlled scale sweep.
rows.check: Compares different model families with different training and input pipelines (logits vs prompt). GPT-4's parameter count is not stated. This is not a scale sweep, so it cannot show whether performance improves with scale.

rows.check: The value is correct. Add the raw per-model numbers: RN50×4 r=0.001 vs RN50×64 r=0.238 at the 25th percentile, a large size gap despite p=0.074.

relationships.reason: The size benefit appears only for high-predictability items (β=0.119, p=0.074) and vanishes at the 90th percentile (β=0.017, p=0.621) (r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: The size effect appeared only for high-predictability items at β=0.119, p=0.074, and vanished at the 90th percentile at β=0.017, p=0.621.

relationships.reason: Size effects are uniformly small and non-significant (largest β=0.103, all p>0.37) over a narrow three-size range (r4).
relationships.display_finding: Size effects were uniformly small and nonsignificant across percentiles, with a largest β of 0.103 and all p-values above 0.37.
